text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Seven former East German civil rights activists quit opposition Greens to join Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
- Construction Minister Klaus Toepfer says 1999 will be the key year in government's move from Bonn to Berlin.
- CDU welcomes text of Czech-German declaration.
- Sluggish investments holding back economic recovery, Bundesbank monthly report says.
- Bunbdesbank also says it will overshoot its money supply target for 1996.
HANDELSBLATT
- Bundesbank demands public spending cuts in 1997.
- Education Minister Juergen Ruettgers says more apprenticeships will be needed in 1997.
- Bundesbank says overvaluation of the mark in 1995 has now been completely corrected.
- Governing coalition hopes to announce timetable for reform of tax system this week.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- German industry provided fewer apprenticeships than agreed for 1996.
- Frankfurt court convicts three founding members of a "pyramid" investment club of fraud.
- Employment in manufacturing industry decreased this year but turnover in the sector is rising.
- Trips to health spas will continue to be covered by public health insurance.
DIE WELT

- CDU deputy parliamentary leader Rudolf Seiters mentioned as possible successor to parliamentary president Rita Suessmuth, who is under pressure over allegations she took advantage of government flights. She denies the accusations.
- Number of deaths from use of drugs rose 11 percent in 1996.
- Costs of government's move from Bonn to Berlin have been lower than expected so far, Toepfer says.
